title: the summit sit
hook: a monk in Chicago opens with "Sisters and Brothers of America", and a quiet teacher on a hill asks one question

segments.voice: Yesterday the summit sit went back to the saints of bhakti, singing in the language of home. Did you say one kind thing in your first language? Today, the modern teachers. Day one thousand fifty.

"Sisters and Brothers of America." Five words, and a monk in an ochre robe has a hall in Chicago listening. That's how Swami Vivekananda began his address there. Far from any podium, on a hill in south India, a quiet teacher named Ramana Maharshi was giving people a question small enough to carry in a pocket. Between those two rooms sit the weeks of the modern teachers: Ramakrishna, Vivekananda, Ramana, Aurobindo, Gandhi, Tagore. Today's summit sit climbs back to them, and sits with the pocket question.
screen: `SISTERS AND BROTHERS OF AMERICA.` → `A HALL, AND A HILL.` → `THE MODERN TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Look back at that block from up here. Ramakrishna, a temple priest whose sayings his followers wrote down. Vivekananda, carrying Vedanta and yoga to lecture halls abroad. Aurobindo writing about the divine at work in ordinary life. Gandhi reading the Gita as a handbook for action without clinging to results. Tagore turning prayer into short poems in Gitanjali. Very different people. And then Ramana, whose central teaching fits in three words: who am I? Here is how the short text called Who Am I? works it, in paraphrase. Thoughts will keep arising. Don't chase them and don't fight them. When one comes, ask: to whom has this thought come? The answer will be: to me. Then ask: who am I? Ramana says the mind then turns back toward its source, and the thought that rose falls quiet. Do this each time, and the questioning itself, he says, wears the other thoughts away, the way a stick used to stir a funeral fire is burned up in the end. That's an unusual picture to leave people with. The question is not a puzzle to solve with a clever answer. Ramana is clear that an answer like "I am this body" doesn't finish it. The question is a tool for turning attention around, from the things that appear to the one they appear to. Across all six teachers, something like that keeps happening: an ancient path, carried into a modern room, made small enough for one person to use.
screen: `SIX TEACHERS, SIX ROOMS.` · `TO WHOM DID THIS THOUGHT COME?` · `TO ME. THEN, WHO AM I?` · `THE STICK THAT STIRS THE FIRE.` · then, large: `TURN ATTENTION AROUND.`

segments.voice: Sit for the bell's two minutes, and let the breath settle. Thoughts will come. That's fine. When one arrives, don't follow it and don't push it away. Ask, quietly: to whom did this come? The answer: to me. Then ask: who am I? Don't answer in words. Just let attention turn back toward the one who is asking, and rest there until the next thought comes. Then the question again. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the modern teachers, and Ramana's question, who am I?
Your line: the summit sit. Today, when a worry shows up, ask it once: to whom did you come? And notice who answers. Day one thousand fifty.

howItsDone: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-inquiry by asking "who am I?" whenever thoughts arise, in sitting practice and in daily life; Vivekananda's addresses and Tagore's Gitanjali are read and recited widely.

original.note: Tamil, in Tamil script: nan yar, who am I? Ramana's question, the name of his short text.

notes: Fourth summit sit (1047–1053): revisits the modern teachers block (937–963).

Vivekananda's opening words are quoted from his own English address (public domain). The script states no date and says only that the hall was 'listening'; the famous ovation is left out because no source is cited for it.

Paraphrase of Who Am I? (Nan Yar?): asking 'to whom did this thought come?', the answer 'to me', then 'who am I?', the mind returning to its source, and the image of the stick used for stirring the funeral pyre. Ramana's text is likely still in copyright in its English translations, so nothing is quoted.
games.original uses Tamil script (நான் யார்) rather than Devanagari, since the question and the text are Tamil; confirm the spelling.
One-line portraits (Ramakrishna's sayings written down by followers; Aurobindo on the divine in ordinary life; Gandhi's Gita as action without clinging) are summaries; confirm.
Editor pass: removed 'I am my job', which was put in Ramana's mouth but is not in Who Am I?; dropped the unsourced 'young'.
